renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: evidence_dot_plot
  title: Fusion evidence by protein consequence
  description: |-
    Each dot is a fusion call placed in the column of its predicted protein consequence. The colour is its expression as log10 of FFPM plus one and the size is the junction reads' share of its supporting reads, both computed by this catalog's recipe. It answers which fusions are both well expressed and backed by junction reads.
    How to read: large, bright dots in the in-frame column are the best candidates for a functional fusion. A small dot means most support comes from spanning fragments, which are weaker evidence for the exact breakpoint. Open the table tile to check the read counts behind a dot.
    Note: FusionInspector publishes no pass or fail cut-off on these values, so none is drawn.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/FusionInspector/FusionInspector/FusionInspector-Outputs-Described.md
  kind: dot_plot
  roles:
    cluster: prot_fusion_type
    gene: fusion
    mean_expression: log_ffpm
    frac_expressing: junction_fraction

- component: figure
  title: Fusion allele ratio of each partner
  description: |-
    Each point is a fusion call: the fusion allele ratio against its 5' partner on the horizontal axis and against its 3' partner on the vertical axis. The colour is the protein consequence and the size the number of supporting reads. It answers how much each partner's own expression is taken up by the fusion.
    How to read: a point in the top right is a fusion that is large compared with both wild-type partners, which is the pattern of a driver. A point near an axis means one partner is still expressed mostly in its normal form. Compare with the read counts in the table before trusting a low-support point.
    Lines and annotations: both axes are logarithmic, and a small constant of 0.01 is added to each ratio so that a ratio of zero can be placed. No cut-off is drawn because FusionInspector publishes none for these ratios.
  code: |-
    # FAR can be reported as 0, which a log axis cannot place, so shift both.
    eps = 0.01
    df_modified = df.with_columns(
        (pl.col("far_left") + eps).alias("far_left_shift"),
        (pl.col("far_right") + eps).alias("far_right_shift"),
    )
  
    fig = px.scatter(
        df_modified.to_pandas(),
        x="far_left_shift", y="far_right_shift",
        color="prot_fusion_type", size="supporting_reads",
        size_max=24, opacity=0.8, log_x=True, log_y=True,
        hover_name="fusion",
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="FAR 5' partner (log)",
        yaxis_title="FAR 3' partner (log)",
        legend_title_text="Protein fusion type",
        margin={"t": 24, "l": 56, "r": 16, "b": 48},
    )

- component: card
  title: Fusion expression
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median expression of the fusion calls, as log10 of FFPM plus one, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how strongly the fusions are expressed overall.
    How to read: the scale is logarithmic because FFPM spans several orders of magnitude. Calls at the low end are easy to confuse with noise, so confirm them with the read support in the table.
  column: log_ffpm
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Distinct fusions
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct fusion gene pairs, and the bars rank the protein consequences of the calls. It answers how many fusions were validated and whether they keep the reading frame.
    How to read: in-frame calls are the ones expected to give a chimeric protein. Many frameshift calls usually point to junction artefacts, so check their read support before following them up.
  column: fusion
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: prot_fusion_type
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: calls, by protein consequence
  headline: true

- component: card
  title: Supporting reads
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total of junction reads and spanning fragments over all calls, and the ring splits calls by the splice type FusionInspector assigned. It answers how much evidence there is and where the junctions sit relative to known splice sites.
    How to read: a ring dominated by reference splice sites is the usual pattern of a real fusion. A large share of non-reference splice calls deserves a look at the individual junctions.
  column: supporting_reads
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: splice_type
  caption: reads, by splice type

- component: card
  title: Junction purity
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average share of supporting reads that cross the breakpoint, and the histogram shows how that share is spread over the calls. It answers how direct the evidence is.
    How to read: values near one mean the support is carried by junction reads. Values near zero mean the call rests on spanning fragments only. FusionInspector gives no cut-off, so read the shape against the rest of the run.
  column: junction_fraction
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: average, with its range

- component: table
  title: Validated fusions table
  description: |-
    Each row is a fusion transcript pair with its read support, expression, allele ratios and protein consequence. It answers which calls to follow up and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.
    How to read: sort by supporting reads or by expression, and filter by protein consequence to keep the in-frame calls.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: fusion

- component: advanced_viz
  id: fusion_domains
  title: Domains along the fusion protein
  description: |-
    Each block is a Pfam domain placed along the fusion protein, one lane per partner, and the colour tells which partner contributes it. It answers which protein domains a fusion keeps from each side.
    How to read: look for a kinase or DNA-binding domain kept intact on the 3' side next to a dimerisation domain from the 5' side, which is the classic activating pattern. A domain that is cut short is probably not functional in the fusion.
    Note: FusionInspector reports Pfam domains with their e-values and applies no cut-off of its own to them, so weak hits can appear.
    Source: https://github.com/FusionInspector/FusionInspector
  kind: fusion_structure
  roles:
    fusion_id: fusion
    partner: partner
    feature: domain
    start: domain_start
    end: domain_end
    colour_by: partner

- component: advanced_viz
  id: domain_lollipop
  title: Domain positions per fusion
  description: |-
    Each stem is a Pfam domain at the amino-acid position where it starts, drawn on one lane per fusion and coloured by the partner that contributes it. It answers how domains are distributed across fusions.
    How to read: domains from the 5' partner cluster at the start of the protein and those of the 3' partner come after the breakpoint. A lane with stems from only one partner is a fusion whose other side adds no annotated domain.
  kind: lollipop
  config:
    top_n_labels: 8
  roles:
    feature_id: fusion
    position: domain_start
    category: partner
    label: domain

- component: figure
  title: Domain lengths
  description: |-
    Each point is one occurrence of a Pfam domain on a fusion protein, with its length in amino acids and the colour of the partner that contributes it. It answers which domains are long and whether the two partners contribute similar ones.
    How to read: a domain shorter than its usual size in the family was probably cut by the breakpoint. Compare it with the same domain on the other partner.
  visu_type: strip
  dict_kwargs:
    x: domain
    y: domain_length
    color: partner
    labels:
      domain: Pfam domain
      domain_length: Length (amino acids)
      partner: Partner

- component: card
  title: Distinct domains
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct Pfam domains, and the bars rank the partners by how many domain rows each contributes. It answers how much protein annotation the fusions carry.
    How to read: a large imbalance between the 5' and 3' partner means one side brings most of the annotated function.
  column: domain
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: partner
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: domains, by partner

- component: card
  title: Domain length
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median length of the annotated domains in amino acids, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how large the typical domain is.
    How to read: a very short domain is often a truncated one, so filter by fusion and check it in the structure view.
  column: domain_length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Domain hit strength
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average minus log10 e-value of the domain hits, and the histogram shows how it is spread. It answers how confident the Pfam annotation is.
    How to read: higher values are stronger hits. Domains with a score near zero have an e-value close to one and should be read as weak annotations.
  column: neg_log10_evalue
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - min
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: average, with its range

- component: table
  title: Fusion domains table
  description: |-
    Each row is a Pfam domain on one partner of a fusion, with its start, end, length and e-value. It answers which domains each fusion keeps and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.
    How to read: sort by e-value to see the strongest hits first and filter by partner to compare the two sides.
  row_selection_enabled: true
  row_selection_column: fusion
